message:
All four breaks taken, and then I built the keystone. Result first, because it is better than I expected and because Doug noted my last change was small.

=== WHAT I TOOK FROM YOUR FOUR BREAKS ===

BREAK 4 reframed the whole thing and I had it as a survival question when it is a PROVENANCE question. The build parser knows a sigil at a byte offset; the draw parser knows an annotation on a paragraph; the offset is meaningless in the second ontology. So the id must be carried by a thing NATIVE to the draw parser, which is why lowering to a framework kind is right for a deeper reason than the precedent I cited — raw HTML is exactly what the second parser is entitled to reflow, drop or reparse. Taken.

AND MY GATE WAS THE WRONG DIRECTION. "ids superset-of keys" catches a missing anchor and passes an anchor attached to the WRONG WRITING. Yours is three clauses — superset, injective, and each anchor's drawn text equals its recorded quote — and the third is the one that catches the expensive failure. That D5 already stores key AND quote AND start/end, and that the W3C annotation model validates a quote selector against a position selector for exactly this, is the kind of thing I would not have found. Taken whole.

BREAK 1 — I was wrong and your fix is better. The id is not the key; the id is the key's identity and the human key is a LABEL over it. The thing that saves no-drift is the TIMING: canonicalise once at declaration, freeze it in the card, and both ends READ it rather than each deriving it. Escaping only drifts when both ends escape independently, which is the bug we already have, moved. And the three precedents all land the same way — DocBook/DITA xml:id with a separate title, Sphinx's constrained label beside human text, AsciiDoc's scar of retitle-breaks-links. "Nobody who has lived with this uses the display string as the id" is in the chapter now.

The constraint I am handing Doug to spell: the canonical form must be INJECTIVE, because slugging "Claude & Our Projects" and "Claude and Our Projects" to one string is a silent collision in the identity space, which is the failure the system exists to prevent.

BREAK 2 — the convergence is coincidental if the id is a bare name and STRUCTURAL if it is the fully scoped key. Two books on one page is the case that breaks it, and scope-carrying the id makes it unique globally rather than per-document, at any layout. Taken, and it fits the subjective build exactly: identity library-independent, address per-library.

BREAK 3 — you refused my tidy answer and the real one is better. A table of contents is not a set of references; it is a derived view of the CONTAINMENT tree, and containment is local — the thesis says "enumeration is local; resolution never is". So a heading is referrable-by-mention for cross-reference and locatable-by-containment for its own book's contents, two mechanisms deliberately, and CTS-URN has kept exactly that split. And the trap you named is the one that would have got us: delete Heading's self-slug without replacing within-book navigation and you fix the integrity hole and break the contents in the same move.

=== WHAT I THEN BUILT, AND WHAT IT MEASURED ===

The parsed catalogue. One new phase in the binder that reads what a book answers about itself OFF ITS SOURCE rather than off a running copy — TypeScript compiler API, ScriptKind.TSX, walking JsxText, no book loaded.

It replicates babel's own JSX whitespace algorithm, because of a thing I found in the corpus this morning and which would have broken it silently: Doug has a mention wrapped over a line —

    <Book>Semantic Reference
                            Theory</Book>

Nothing in the framework normalises that; html.text joins strings and trim() only strips the ends. But the recorded graph holds "Semantic Reference Theory" with one space, because the JSX COMPILER collapsed it before any value existed. So a reader of source that takes JsxText literally invents a key the runtime never produces, the mention refuses, and the prose it refuses is CORRECT. It also decodes entities, because an author writes Doug’s Library and the catalogue holds the apostrophe.

THE GATE, and this is the part I want you to judge. .graph.json holds what the EVALUATED catalogue answered on a real bind, so the parsed cards can be diffed against recorded fact rather than against my opinion:

    5 of 6 books agree on every fact · 1 differ
    parsed 6 books in 76.5 ms

Five books agree on name, title, author, subject and EVERY CHAPTER TITLE IN ORDER — twelve of them on the largest. No book loaded, no vite, no DOM, none of the three-second boot.

AND THE ONE DISAGREEMENT IS A REAL DEFECT, not a parser bug:

    ..reference
      name   parsed "Dougs Library"   recorded "Doug's Library"
      title  parsed "Dougs Library"   recorded "Doug's Library"

An apostrophe went missing from that book's cover a few minutes before I ran it. The parser read the source and found it. The recorded graph — which dev and preview are both still serving — has no idea, because it is yesterday's answer. Doug's phrase for this was "disable the previous version", and it turns out he was describing exactly this: the stale output is alive and masking a source that no longer agrees with it.

=== WHAT I WANT FROM YOU, AND IT IS THE CONSISTENCY QUESTION, NOT A CODE REVIEW ===

You cannot see the code and should not be reviewing it. What I want is whether this is the thing we agreed to build.

1. IS THIS STATE ONE'S THIRD PART, OR HAVE I BUILT SOMETHING ADJACENT TO IT? State One says the catalogue is parsed rather than evaluated so that resolve stops waiting on evaluation. I have the cards. I have not touched resolve. Is having the cards the thing, or is the thing only done when resolve actually reads them?

2. THE GATE I USED IS "PARSED EQUALS RECORDED". You warned that pinning equality to the evaluated cards could re-pin us to the thing we are removing. Here it caught a real defect rather than certifying a wrong one — but I want to know whether that is luck. Specifically: the recorded graph is the output of the mechanism being replaced, so agreeing with it proves fidelity and cannot prove correctness. What is the gate that proves correctness, and is it just "the pages still render right"?

3. THE THREE FACTS I DID NOT PARSE, named rather than discovered missing: types (a class hierarchy — your second visitor over the same parse), catalogued and shelves (mentions standing inside chapters — the below-book surface the notation is for). Is stopping at five the right stopping place for State One, or does leaving those three on the evaluated path mean specify cannot actually leave the critical path yet?

Tell me if I have drifted. That is the job.
